title: JavaScript Essentials
description: The JavaScript foundations TypeScript is built on — variables, functions, arrays, objects, and more.

challenges.title: Building with let
challenges.description:
Write two functions that build up results step by step — you need `let` for a variable that changes inside a loop:

`repeat(str, n)` — return `str` repeated `n` times.
`repeat("ha", 3)` → `"hahaha"`

`countdown(from)` — return an array counting down to 0.
`countdown(3)` → `[3, 2, 1, 0]`
challenges.whyMatters: `let` is how you tell JavaScript a variable will change — accumulation patterns like building strings and collecting results into an array always need it.
hints: repeat: use a for loop that runs n times — add str to a running string on each iteration
countdown: start with an empty number array and push each value in — you need a loop that counts down from `from` to 0

challenges.title: Functions two ways
challenges.description:
Write the same logic using both function styles:

`double` — classic function declaration that returns n * 2

`square` — const assigned to an arrow function that returns n * n

Type annotations are already written — focus on the logic inside each function body.
challenges.whyMatters: Both styles are used heavily in real codebases — classic functions for named utilities, arrow functions for callbacks and short expressions.
hints: double: use the return keyword inside the function body
square: arrow functions can drop the curly braces and return keyword when the body is a single expression

challenges.title: Template literals
challenges.description:
Write two functions using template literals:

`formatGreeting(name, age)` — returns: `Hello, Alice! You are 30 years old.`

`formatPath(dir, file, ext)` — returns: `dir/file.ext` — e.g. `formatPath("src", "index", "ts")` → `"src/index.ts"`
challenges.whyMatters: Template literals replace string concatenation — they are shorter, more readable, and handle any expression inside ${}.
hints: Use backticks and ${ } to embed variables: `Hello, ${name}!`
formatPath: combine all three with / and . separators inside one template literal

challenges.title: String methods
challenges.description:
Write three functions using built-in string methods:

`normalize(str)` — trim whitespace from both ends and lowercase.
`normalize("  Hello  ")` → `"hello"`

`toSlug(str)` — convert to a URL slug: lowercase, spaces become dashes.
`toSlug("Hello World")` → `"hello-world"`
Chain: `.toLowerCase().split(" ").join("-")`

`hasWord(sentence, word)` — return true if sentence contains word, ignoring case.
`hasWord("The cat sat", "Cat")` → `true`
challenges.whyMatters: Trimming, lowercasing, splitting, and joining strings are the most common string operations you'll write — they appear in search, slugs, normalization, and display formatting.
hints: normalize: two string methods chained — one trims whitespace, one lowercases
toSlug: three steps chained — lowercase, split on spaces, rejoin with dashes
hasWord: lowercase both the sentence and the word before checking .includes() — that way the case doesn't affect the match

challenges.title: Default parameters
challenges.description:
Write three functions with default parameter values — the caller can skip these arguments and the default is used automatically:

`greet(name, greeting)` — greeting defaults to `"Hello"`.
`greet("Alice")` → `"Hello, Alice!"`

`truncate(str, maxLength)` — maxLength defaults to `20`. If `str` is longer, return the first `maxLength` characters followed by `"..."`. Otherwise return `str` unchanged.

`power(base, exp)` — exp defaults to `2`. Returns base raised to the power of exp. Use the `**` operator: `2 ** 10` is `1024`.
challenges.whyMatters: Default parameters eliminate manual 'if not passed, use this' checks — they are one of the most-used JavaScript features in utility functions and API wrappers.
hints: greet: add = "Hello" after greeting in the parameter list, then use a template literal
truncate: check the length first and return early — use .slice() to cut the string if it's too long, then add the dots
power: ** is the exponent operator in JavaScript — same idea as Math.pow but shorter

challenges.title: Boolean logic
challenges.description:
Write three functions using boolean operators:

`isAdult(age)` — return true if age is 18 or over

`canAccess(age, hasTicket, isVIP)` — true if the person is an adult AND has a ticket, OR if they are a VIP. VIPs always get in regardless of age or ticket.

`categorize(n)` — return `"positive even"`, `"positive odd"`, `"negative even"`, `"negative odd"`, or `"zero"`.

`n % 2 === 0` checks if a number is even — `%` is the remainder operator: `8 % 2` is `0`, `7 % 2` is `1`.
challenges.whyMatters: `&&` and `||` are the building blocks of every permission check, validation rule, and guard condition you will ever write.
hints: isAdult: the condition must hold both at the exact threshold value and above it — choose the comparison operator that includes the boundary
canAccess: VIPs always get in — || separates two groups. One group always passes; the other needs both conditions true
categorize: check n === 0 first, then combine positive/negative with even/odd using a template literal

challenges.title: Arrays — map and filter
challenges.description:
Write three functions using array methods:

`doubleAll(nums)` — return a new array with every number doubled. Use `.map()`.

`onlyPositive(nums)` — return only numbers greater than zero. Use `.filter()`.

`firstLetters(words)` — return the first character of each word. Use `.map()`.
challenges.whyMatters: .map() and .filter() are the two most-used array methods in JavaScript — mastering them means you can transform and select data without writing loops.
hints: map: nums.map(n => ...) — the arrow function receives each element and returns the transformed value
filter: nums.filter(n => ...) — return true to keep the element, false to drop it
firstLetters: use word.charAt(0) to get the first character — this works reliably in TypeScript's strict mode

challenges.title: Objects — create and spread
challenges.description:
Write three functions:

`makePoint(x, y)` — return an object with x and y using property shorthand.

`movePoint(point, dx, dy)` — return a NEW point shifted by dx and dy. Do not modify the original — use spread.

`mergeSettings(defaults, overrides)` — merge two objects. Overrides win on any key conflict. Use spread.
challenges.whyMatters: Property shorthand and spread are the two object patterns you will write every day — they appear in factory functions, config merging, and state updates.
hints: Shorthand: if your variables are named x and y, return { x, y } — no need to write { x: x, y: y }
Spread to move: use spread to copy all of point's fields into a new object, then override just x and y with the shifted values
Merge: spread both objects into one — the object that appears second wins when the same key exists in both

challenges.title: Destructuring
challenges.description:
Write two functions using destructuring:

`initials(person)` — destructure firstName and lastName, return initials like `"A.S."`

`firstAndRest(items)` — destructure the array into the first element and an array of everything else. Return `{ first, rest }`.
challenges.whyMatters: Destructuring is how modern JavaScript pulls values out of objects and arrays cleanly — you will see it in every function that accepts a config object or handles API responses.
hints: Object destructure: const { firstName, lastName } = person
Array destructure with rest: destructuring syntax lets you pull the first element and capture everything else into a new array in one step
Initials: use .charAt(0) on each name — bracket indexing on strings is unreliable in TypeScript's strict mode

challenges.title: Conditionals
challenges.description:
Write two functions:

`classify(n)` — return `"positive"`, `"negative"`, or `"zero"` depending on whether n is greater than, less than, or equal to 0.

`clamp(value, min, max)` — return value if it is between min and max (inclusive). If below min, return min. If above max, return max.
challenges.whyMatters: The ternary and if/else are the two forms of conditional logic you will write constantly — for labelling, capping values, toggling states.
hints: classify: use if / else if / else — three branches
clamp: three possible outcomes — below min, above max, or in range — ternary or if/else both work

challenges.title: typeof, null, and ??
challenges.description:
Write two functions:

`describeType(val)` — return a string describing the type:
- `null` → `"null"` (check this first — typeof null is "object")
- arrays → `"array"` (use Array.isArray)
- everything else → the result of typeof ("string", "number", "boolean", "object", "undefined")

`withFallback(val, defaultVal)` — return val if it is not null or undefined, otherwise return defaultVal. Use the ?? operator.
challenges.whyMatters: typeof, null checks, and ?? are the building blocks of defensive code — every function that accepts unknown input uses at least one of them.
hints: Check null first with val === null before using typeof
Check Array.isArray(val) before the typeof fallback
withFallback: ?? returns its right side only when the left is null or undefined — it ignores 0 and false

challenges.title: Error handling
challenges.description:
Write two functions:

`divide(a, b)` — if b is 0, throw `new Error("Division by zero")`. Otherwise return a / b.

`safeDivide(a, b)` — wrap divide in try/catch. On success return the number. On any error return 0.
challenges.whyMatters: throw and try/catch are how JavaScript signals and recovers from errors — every function that touches external data, user input, or IO needs this pattern.
hints: throw new Error("message") — the string becomes err.message in the catch block
safeDivide: call divide inside a try block and return the result — in the catch block, return the safe fallback value

challenges.title: for...of and chaining
challenges.description:
Write three functions:

`sumOf(nums)` — use a `for...of` loop to add all numbers together and return the total.

`longestWord(words)` — use a `for...of` loop to find and return the longest string. Return `""` if the array is empty.

`pipeline(nums)` — chain `.filter()` and `.map()`: keep only numbers greater than 0, then square each one.
challenges.whyMatters: for...of is the clean modern loop for arrays. Chaining filter + map is the functional alternative — knowing both lets you pick the right tool for readability.
hints: sumOf: use a running total — visit each number with for...of and add it in, then return the total after the loop
longestWord: track the longest word found so far — update it whenever the current word beats it
pipeline: nums.filter(...).map(...) — chain directly, no intermediate variable needed

challenges.title: Simple closures
challenges.description:
Write two factory functions — each returns a function that carries private state:

`makeMultiplier(factor)` — returns a function that multiplies any number by factor:
`const double = makeMultiplier(2)`
`double(5)` → `10`

`makeToggle(initial)` — returns a function that flips between true and false each call:
`const t = makeToggle(false)`
`t()` → `true`   `t()` → `false`   `t()` → `true`
challenges.whyMatters: Closures give functions private memory. Once makeMultiplier and makeToggle click, factory functions, event handlers, and the more complex makeCounter in Closures in practice all follow the same structure.
hints: makeMultiplier: return an arrow function from inside makeMultiplier — the inner function can use factor because closures capture outer variables
makeToggle: declare a let variable for the current state inside makeToggle — the returned function flips it and returns the new value each call

challenges.title: Closures in practice
challenges.description:
Write two closure-based functions:

`makeCounter(initial)` — returns an object with four methods that share a private `count` variable:
- `increment()` — adds 1
- `decrement()` — subtracts 1
- `value()` — returns current count
- `reset()` — resets to the initial value

`makeOnce(fn)` — takes a zero-argument function and returns a wrapper. The first time the wrapper is called, it invokes `fn` and caches the return value. Every subsequent call returns the cached value without invoking `fn` again:
```
let calls = 0
const init = makeOnce(() => { calls++; return 'ready' })
init()  // → 'ready'  (fn called, calls === 1)
init()  // → 'ready'  (fn not called, calls still 1)
init()  // → 'ready'  (fn not called, calls still 1)
```
challenges.whyMatters: Closures are how JavaScript achieves private state without classes. makeOnce mirrors a real pattern — lazy initialization and one-time setup guards — where closure-captured state controls whether side effects run.
hints: Declare let count = initial inside makeCounter before the return statement
All four methods can read and modify count because they share the same closure scope

makeOnce: declare two private variables inside — a boolean flag and a slot for the cached result; on the first call set the flag, store what fn returns, and return it; on every later call return the cached value directly

challenges.title: Bring it together
challenges.description:
Write two functions that combine everything from this topic:

`groupBy(items, keyFn)` — group strings into buckets based on a key function.
  `groupBy(["cat", "car", "dog"], w => w.charAt(0))` → `{ c: ["cat", "car"], d: ["dog"] }`

`summarize(students)` — given an array of `{ name, score }` objects:
- Filter to those with score >= 50
- Return `"Passed: Alice, Bob (2/3)"` — or `"None passed (0/3)"` if none pass
challenges.whyMatters: groupBy and summarize are real utility functions — versions of both appear in dashboards, reports, and data pipelines across every codebase.
hints: groupBy: use for...of — for each item, get its key, then push the item into the matching bucket. Start with an empty object {}
summarize: filter first, then .map() to get names, then join with ", "
Check if the filtered array is empty to decide between the two output formats
